As someone who spent a few years in a cabin, the first practical thing to consider is space management and storage.  Storage storage storage.  (There are many books and other resources on practical and/or unique storage ideas - read/watch them all.)
And consider your environment when contemplating that storage.  If you live in a place where the summers can be wet and the winters below zero (like Alaska) factor that into your storage spaces, especially any with an outside wall.  Without air circulation (at least 2” space), freezing and/or condensation can be an issue that can result in mildew or mold growth.

comments.text:
Watch out for, the Influencer- Influence lies.😂😂
The real problem is people paying hundreds of thousands of dollars for a prefab tiny home—that is just FOMO for rich people.
I finished my repossessed 324 sq ft shed (an older 2x4, 16" on-center BetterBuilt model, which is sturdier than what they make now). It sits 150 feet from the main property. I have been working on it for 3 years…of scavenging Habitat for Humanity ReStores, scouring cull lumber racks, and buying damaged sales to get it done. If you want to save money, you buy only what you absolutely HAVE to. The 1st woman can drop a Cat6A Ethernet line, put your earplugs in, lather then rinse and commit.
For the big things, I hire licensed, bonded professionals. Everything is documented in writing to stay strictly to code—not just for safety, but for insurance peace of mind. You have to live like a disaster could happen tomorrow, but you don't gamble with your setup. It takes money (or a strong support system) to save money. If you can't cut out the excess and sweat out the labor, be comfortable with existing under someone else's rules.
If you look closely, affordable "tiny homes" are already hidden on-grid all over the nation. Often, it is significantly cheaper to buy actual real estate than to deal with the zoning, access, and waste-void nightmares of a mobile tiny home. You just have to think outside the box and beat the fad-induced inflation:
Location Strategy: Look for inexpensive homes near freeway buffers, railroads, or eminent domain lines. They aren't always bad neighborhoods, just unglamorous.
The Ideal Fixer-Upper: Find the least expensive house in a nice neighborhood. Look for old company houses, veteran program homes, or historic Sears kits. Try neighborhoods with homes that; e.g. needs curb appeal,"in-the-dry", has solid foundation, no abandoned property or heavy unstructured traffic with space to safely store your tools.
Smart Scouting: Buy it while you still have a stable place to live. Visit the property at different times of the day, week, and especially during heavy rain.
Rigorous Inspection: Learn to hunt for hidden damage. Sniff out dampness or pet odors. Check if exterior foliage is touching wood or sills. Trace past leaks by inspecting adjacent  roof, walls and ceilings. When you hire a professional for structural,electrical and inspections, find one you can trust implicitly—then show up unannounced to check their work.
Deep dive, buy a house,DIY what you can, but know when to call the pros. Budget time (yours and city regs.) and include unexpected costs and delays. and supplies.

comments.text: Yes I would buy a tiny home and no its not for everyone. I think here...people assume a tiny home is a regular sticks and bricks house. Americans love to buy tons of shyt and they complain about everything is so expensive and they dont have money but constantly buy from Temu or Shein. Learn to focus on living intentionally and guess what you start putting money towards better products. I dont follow trends..I try to focus on timeless things and I prefer to save up money to buy let's say a pair of boots that are expensive in lieu of buying 20 pairs of different boots because it was a good deal that $60 pair and its what is trending. I am going to pay a chunk of bills for my custom tiny home but it will work for my lifestyle. I dont need big kitchens and big appliances hence why I'm going custom.
